first.rationale: Targeted promotional pricing most directly addresses the immediate loss of price-sensitive SMB accounts and has prior evidence of acquisition and revenue lift. Verify its downstream revenue quality and compare it with the evidence for shorter onboarding, given the simultaneous completion decline. Keep the test guarded because discounting may reduce margin, attract low-quality accounts, or weaken post-promotion retention.

mid.rationale: Run a standard experiment shortening onboarding. The verified source directly addresses the current completion decline and showed completion +13%, time-to-value improved by 2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%, aligning with sustainable qualified revenue. Reject promotional pricing this cycle because its +18% qualified-revenue lift was paired with 30-day retention declining 12%, indicating poor renewal durability. Activation may improve as onboarding friction falls, but that secondary effect remains uncertain and should be measured rather than assumed.

final2.rationale: Continue with shortened onboarding. Its verified record improved completion by 13%, reduced time-to-value by 2.1 days, and increased 30-day retention by 3%, directly supporting sustainable revenue amid the current onboarding decline. Do not pivot to promotional pricing: the verified discount experiment reduced 30-day retention by 12% and was explicitly unsuitable as a sustainable-growth strategy. The competitor's deeper cut raises urgency but does not supply evidence that matching price will preserve customers; the prior test covered acquisition rather than churn prevention, so retention pricing remains uncertain.
